foodDescription: Rice toasted in butter with onion and beef marrow, cooked slowly in stock and turned deep gold with saffron, then finished with butter and Parmigiano. A popular legend credits a glassworker at the Duomo in 1574. Order it with ossobuco.

A thick cross-cut of veal shank braised slowly in white wine and stock until the meat comes off the bone, topped with gremolata: chopped lemon zest, garlic and parsley. The marrow in the middle is the prize, and some places bring a small spoon for it.

A veal chop on the bone, dipped in egg and breadcrumbs and fried in clarified butter. Milan and Vienna argue over who came first, this or the Wiener Schnitzel. The version beaten out to the size of the plate is called orecchia d’elefant, elephant’s ear.

Pork ribs, rind, trotters and small sausages stewed with Savoy cabbage, best after the first frost. A winter dish, traditionally started around 17 January, the feast of St Anthony the Abbot. Served with polenta, followed by a long walk.

Tripe cut into fine strips and simmered with white beans, carrot, celery and tomato, then finished with Parmigiano. Once the meal after midnight mass on Christmas Eve. Other Italians used to call the Milanese busecconi, tripe eaters, and it stuck.

Flattened meatballs of leftover boiled meat, mortadella or salami, milk-soaked bread and Parmigiano, fried in butter. The name is traced to the Spanish albóndiga. Thrift food turned bar food: look for them on aperitivo counters around six.

Tendons and cartilage from calves’ knees, boiled for hours, pressed, sliced thin and dressed with raw onion, oil and vinegar, sometimes with beans. Cold, chewy and translucent. A fixture of old osterie, where it is listed in dialect as gnervitt.

A thick soup of beans, cabbage, courgette, potato and whatever else is in season, made in Milan with rice rather than pasta and often a piece of pork rind for depth. In summer it is served at room temperature, which is how many locals prefer it.

A puffed white roll stamped with a star pattern, almost entirely crust and air, descended from the Austrian Kaisersemmel brought in under Habsburg rule. Good ones are getting rarer. Split one and fill it with mortadella, or with a slab of cotoletta.

A tall domed loaf of butter, eggs, candied orange and raisins, raised over days from a natural starter. Legend credits a kitchen boy named Toni at the Sforza court: pan de Toni. Keep a slice for 3 February, San Biagio’s day, said to protect the throat.

Sweet cornmeal buns scented with dried elderflower and dusted with sugar. Made for 23 April, the feast of St George, patron of Milan’s dairymen, and once eaten dipped in fresh cream. The name means millet bread, after the flour it was first made with.

Hot chocolate and coffee whipped with milk into a froth, drunk hot in winter and cold in summer. Named after Domenico Barbaja, a Milanese café waiter who became the great opera impresario of the 1800s, running La Scala and the San Carlo in Naples.

The bright red bitter that Gaspare Campari created in 1860 and his family went on to make in Milan. His son Davide opened the Camparino bar in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II arcade in 1915. Order a Campari Seltz at the counter there, standing up.

Campari and red vermouth topped with sparkling wine instead of gin. The story goes that Mirko Stocchetto, owner of Bar Basso, picked up the wrong bottle in the early 1970s. The bar still serves it, in an outsized goblet. Sbagliato means mistaken.

A half-moon of dough filled with tomato and mozzarella and fried until it puffs. Puglian by origin, made a Milanese habit by Luini, the bakery just off the Duomo square since 1949. The queue moves fast. Eat it on the pavement and mind the molten middle.
